lesson_title: Lift a Minibus With One Arm
hook_text: No lever, no gears. Just oil in a tube. How does one arm lift a loaded taxi?
clip_script: At the back of a Durban taxi rank a mechanic slides a trolley jack under a minibus, pumps a handle, and the whole vehicle rises. Oil does it. Push a small piston into oil and the pressure spreads through every drop of it, all the way to a much bigger piston under the lifting arm. Same pressure, bigger face, bigger force. If the big piston is fifty times the area, it pushes fifty times harder. That is hydraulics, and it is a mechanical advantage with no lever. The catch: the big piston moves fifty times less, so the mechanic pumps and pumps. Why oil and not air? Block a syringe of air and push: it squashes and springs back. Block a syringe of water: it will not budge. Air is for hissing bus doors and soft tyres. Liquid is for brakes, diggers and the Jaws of Life, which must hold a car door open without bouncing. Two syringes and water: that is your rescue device.
visual_style: Whiteboard cross-section of two cylinders joined by a tube, small piston down, large piston up with a minibus on it; inset of air and water syringes being pushed.
mood: Wonder at a simple trick, then the clear reason behind it.
pacing: Hook at the jack, slow walk through pressure and area, fast contrast of air versus water.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and try the blocked-syringe test with air and with water.
